title: DynamoDB: a table you never have to run
dek: DynamoDB is a key-value and document store where you never pick a server size, patch an engine or plan a failover. You pay for that with discipline: every query must use a key you designed in advance, and every partition has its own limit. Here is how keys, indexes, capacity and consistency work.

items: Every item has a partition key and an optional sort key. Queries fetch one partition, optionally a range of its sort key; anything else is a full-table Scan.
Global secondary indexes copy items under another key, asynchronously, so other questions can be answered by key too.
Capacity is per partition as well as per table: about 1,000 writes and 3,000 reads a second per partition. One hot key gets throttled even when the table has room.

body.cap: Design the keys from the questions: the table answers one, each index answers another. A question with no matching key is a scan.

items: Partition key only: get one item by ID, such as a session or a rider's latest location.
Partition key plus sort key: get a range inside a partition, such as a customer's orders between two dates, in order.
Items are up to 400 KB; bigger things go to object storage with the key in the item.
Some teams keep several entity types in one table with generic key names (single-table design) so one Query returns related items together. It is efficient, and harder to read and change.
Global secondary indexes have their own partition and sort keys and their own capacity. They are updated asynchronously, so reads from them are always eventually consistent.
Local secondary indexes share the table's partition key with a different sort key; they must be created with the table and limit each partition key's data to 10 GB.
Each index copies the attributes you project into it, so storage and write costs grow with every index.

body.cap: The table's total capacity hides a per-partition limit. A key that everyone writes to is throttled, and the fix is in the key design, not in buying more capacity.

items: On-demand mode bills per request and absorbs changes in traffic; provisioned mode is cheaper for steady load and can autoscale.
A read unit covers a strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second, or two eventually consistent ones; a write unit covers one write of up to 1 KB.
Adaptive capacity shifts throughput to busy partitions, but it can't take one partition past its own limit. Spread hot keys with a suffix and combine on read.
Throttled requests come back with an error; SDKs retry with backoff, which hides short bursts and makes long ones slow.
Reads are eventually consistent by default; ask for a strongly consistent read and pay twice the read units, within one region.
Conditional writes (`attribute_not_exists`, a version check) make compare-and-set safe without locks.
Transactions group up to 100 actions across items and tables, all or nothing, at twice the cost of normal writes.
Global tables replicate across regions; by default concurrent writes to the same item are resolved by last writer wins.
Streams record every change for 24 hours, so a function or consumer can update search, caches or counters: change-data capture built in.
TTL deletes expired items for free, usually within a few days of expiry, so don't rely on it for exact timing.
Backups and point-in-time recovery are settings, not projects.
Write the key schema for each access pattern: table keys first, then each index and the question it answers.
Check every key for heat: a celebrity, a match, today's date.
Say where you need strong reads or conditional writes, and where eventual is fine.
Name the stream for anything derived: search index, counters, notifications.

body.x: On-demand suits new products and spiky traffic: no planning, no throttling from mis-set capacity, a higher price per request. Provisioned with autoscaling is cheaper once traffic is steady and known, but autoscaling reacts in minutes, so a sudden spike can be throttled first. Many teams start on-demand and switch tables to provisioned once a few months of traffic show the pattern.
